analysis.one_liner: Requires remote-control valves and leak-detection systems on hazardous liquid pipelines near cities and waterways.
analysis.headline: The pipeline safety bill got a House subcommittee hearing but never a vote, dying when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write rules requiring pipeline companies to install remote-control valves and computerized leak-detection systems on hazardous liquid pipelines in major urban and suburban areas and near wide water crossings, drinking-water reservoirs, and larger streams. Companies would also have had to report the environmental effects of pipeline leaks, with that information made public. Existing pipelines would have had until January 1, 1997 to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near hazardous liquid pipelines in cities and suburbs, communities whose drinking water comes from reservoirs or rivers crossed by pipelines, and the environment generally. Faster shut-off of leaking lines and earlier leak detection mean fewer fires, explosions, and contaminated water supplies after a pipeline rupture.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near urban pipelines and water crossings

how_it_helps.text: Requires remote control valves at intervals of no more than 5 miles on pipelines in metropolitan areas and on both sides of water crossings over 100 feet wide, drinking-water reservoirs, and streams with significant flow, so operators can cut off a leaking line remotely [S3].

Requires supervisory control and data acquisition systems with leak detection subsystems on the same pipeline facilities, with regulations due within 6 months and installation required by January 1, 1997 for existing lines [S3].

Requires pipeline operators to report the environmental effects of reportable leaks — water pollution, soil contamination, harm to wildlife and waterfowl — and directs the Secretary to make that information available to other agencies and to the public on request [S3].
Directs the Secretary to assess extending valve and leak-detection requirements to other pipelines in locations posing substantial risk to public safety, property, wildlife, or the environment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline companies that carry hazardous liquids. They would bear the cost of buying and installing remote-control valves and leak-detection systems on lines in urban areas and near water crossings by 1997, and the paperwork of environmental-impact reporting after leaks.

drawbacks.text: Compliance deadlines were aggressive: rules within 6 months of enactment and full installation on existing pipelines by January 1, 1997, which could be costly for operators and might raise shipping costs that get passed into fuel and product prices [S3].
The bill left the technical standards to later regulation by the Secretary of Transportation, so the actual stringency and cost would depend on rules written after passage [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the highest-risk lines — those running through metropolitan areas and near drinking water — rather than every pipeline, which limits the cost while concentrating the safety benefit. The main honest objection is cost: retrofitting valves and monitoring systems is expensive, and some of that cost would flow into prices. Against that is the potential damage from a single urban pipeline rupture.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to subcommittees, got one hearing in September 1991, and never moved further before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the bill on June 10, 1991 [S1].
It was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Public Works and Transportation Committee [S1].
It was sent to the Surface Transportation Subcommittee and the Energy and Power Subcommittee in June and July 1991, and the Department of Transportation was asked for its comments [S1].
A subcommittee hearing was held on September 25, 1991 — the last action of any kind before the Congress ended [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators avoided mandated valve and leak-detection installations; residents near urban pipelines and water crossings went without the safety protections.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Pipeline Act of 1991 to require remote-control valves and leak-detection systems on hazardous liquid pipelines in urban areas and near water crossings.

for.name: House Surface Transportation Subcommittee
for.role: Subcommittee, Public Works and Transportation Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on September 25, 1991.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and referred it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee; no markup or floor action followed.

against.name: House Committee on Public Works and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and referred it to the Surface Transportation Subcommittee; after a single hearing, the bill saw no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no party split is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have required operators to install remote-control valves and leak-detection systems on urban and water-crossing pipelines by 1997, plus environmental reporting after leaks. Its death spared them that retrofit cost while leaving nearby residents without the safety protections.

industries.industry: Pipeline equipment manufacturers (valves and control systems)
industries.note: Mandated installation of remote-control valves and SCADA systems would have created a large compliance market for these products. The bill's death removed that demand.
